doc.title: Vince Lateano interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Tjader as a Latin jazz pioneer
summary: Tjader's Latin jazz idea after hearing Tito Puente and Machito, and the early Latin jazz pioneers; John Santos recommended.

blocks.x: One of the first to really popularize the kind of world music type.

He was a pioneer, yeah, he was. He was working with George Shearing — Cal was from here, from the West Coast, he’s from San Mateo, which is down the Peninsula. He and Merv Griffin went to prep school or high school together, so they were buddies. But anyway Cal, kind of a self-taught player, but worked with George Shearing for a while and while he was with George Shearing in New York, Al McKibbon was on the band and Al took him around the corner to the Palladium one night and he heard Tito Puente and Machito playing in a ballroom and flipped. And he just never heard anything like that he said. And so he got this idea that when he came back here after he left Shearing to put a © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

Latin jazz thing together, which is what he did. He had guys from here that could play both, because they had to play both ways. And then he said that they would barnstorm, where they would get in a car and go across the country and work all these places between here and New York where they had never heard anything like that, never heard Latin music. In fact he ran into some resistance in some places he said, they didn’t want to hear that. And so he was a pioneer. Of course I think Dizzy was the first guy — or actually was it Mario Bauza, is he the guy that—
He was with Dizzy, wasn’t he?
Well I think he was with Machito.
But I’m talking about Latin jazz. I think Dizzy with Chano Pozo was the first real jazz musician to cross over like that. But you know a guy you should talk to is John Santos. Has his name come up?

He lives in the Bay area, he’s a Latin musician, but he’s a walking history book. He’s a real interesting in the history of the music. But yeah, Cal was a pioneer, until I guess — I’m trying to think of what put him on the map. I guess “Soul Sauce/Guachi Guaro” was the first real national kind of hit in the early 60s. And I was with him in 1980, he won a Grammy. And I was on that record, which was sort of a —
